Measurement Error Test

Source: R/reli_err_test.R
reli_err_test.Rd

Estimates one measurement error statistic, the standard error of measurement (SEM), the standard error of estimate (SEE), or the standard error of prediction (SEP), with a confidence interval and an optional test against an acceptable error, and returns an object of class "htest". The defaults give the typical error of Hopkins (2000): the SEM from a two-way model with systematic differences between items excluded, \(\sqrt{MS_E}\).

Usage

reli_err_test(
  x = NULL,
  data = NULL,
  measure = NULL,
  item = NULL,
  id = NULL,
  col.names = NULL,
  stat = c("SEM", "SEE", "SEP"),
  scale = c("raw", "log", "mean"),
  model = c("twoway", "oneway"),
  type = c("consistency", "agreement"),
  method = c("anova", "reml"),
  conf.level = 0.95,
  null.value = NULL,
  alternative = c("less", "greater", "two.sided"),
  boot = FALSE,
  boot_ci = c("auto", "perc", "bca", "stud", "basic"),
  replicates = 1999,
  se_method = c("jackknife", "influence", "normal")
)

Arguments

x

A formula of the form values ~ item | id, where values is the measurement, item identifies the trial, rater or occasion, and id identifies the subject. Use either x, the measure/item/id arguments, or col.names.

data

A data frame containing the variables.

measure, item, id

Column names (character) of the measurement, the item (trial, rater, or occasion) and the subject identifier, for data in long format.

col.names

Column names (character) of the items, for data in wide format (one row per subject).

stat

"SEM" (default), "SEE", or "SEP". See Details.

scale

The scale the statistic is reported on: "raw" (default, units of the measurement), "log" (sympercents: 100 times the statistic of the log-transformed measurements), or "mean" (percentage of the grand mean). The last two are coefficients of variation; see Details.

model

"twoway" (default) when every subject is measured on the same set of items (e.g. test-retest trials), or "oneway" when each subject is measured by a different set of items.

type

"consistency" (default) excludes systematic differences between items from the error; "agreement" includes them. Only "agreement" is defined for model = "oneway".

method

"anova" (default) estimates the variance components from the analysis of variance and requires complete, balanced data. "reml" fits a linear mixed model and allows missing measurements.

conf.level

Confidence level of the interval (default 0.95).

null.value

An acceptable error to test against, on the scale given by scale (units, sympercents, or percent of the mean). The default, NULL, gives the estimate and interval without a test.

alternative

"less" (default), "greater", or "two.sided". The default tests whether the error is smaller than null.value. Used only when null.value is given; without a test the interval is two-sided.

boot

If TRUE, use a nonparametric bootstrap that resamples subjects for the interval and p-value. Default FALSE.

boot_ci

Bootstrap interval type: "auto" (default), "perc" (percentile), "bca", "stud" (studentized), or "basic". With method = "anova", "auto" uses "bca" for the two-way agreement statistics and "stud" otherwise ("perc" when se_method = "normal"); with method = "reml" it uses "perc". See Details. Used only when boot = TRUE.

replicates

Number of bootstrap replicates (default 1999).

se_method

How the standard error of the log of the statistic is estimated: "jackknife" (default; delete one subject at a time, accurate in simulations but n refits with method = "reml"), "influence" (a per-subject sandwich estimate; cheap but too small with few subjects), or "normal" (normal theory; too small with skewed or heavy-tailed data, and cannot be used by the studentized bootstrap). It is reported in stderr and used by the studentized bootstrap; it does not change the analytic interval or test. For the two-way agreement statistics, the jackknife and influence SEs add the normal-theory variance of the item mean square, treating the items as random (as the hybrid bootstrap does). See icc_test() for the simulations.

Value

A list of class c("reli_htest", "htest") containing:

statistic

The \(\chi^2\) (SEM) or z (SEE, SEP) statistic, when a test was requested without the bootstrap.

parameter

The degrees of freedom of the \(\chi^2\) test.

p.value

The p-value, when a test was requested.

conf.int

The confidence interval.

estimate

The estimate, named by stat.

stderr

Standard errors of the estimate (named by stat) and of its log (log), from se_method. With boot = TRUE, also boot: the standard deviation of the bootstrap estimates.

null.value

The acceptable error tested against, if any.

alternative

The alternative hypothesis.

method

A description of the statistic and the inference.

data.name

A description of the data.

fit

The fitted variance components, mean squares and model.

data

The data in long format.

settings

The settings used, for the methods.

boot

Bootstrap details (NULL unless boot = TRUE).

Details

Choosing model and type. Choose them as for the ICC (see "Choosing the form" in icc_test()): type = "agreement" when systematic differences between items count as error, "consistency" when they are checked and reported separately. Report the error statistic that matches the ICC.

Statistics. With \(MS\) the mean squares of the subjects-by-items analysis of variance (n subjects, k items):

statmodeltypeEstimateAnalytic inference
SEMtwowayconsistency\(\sqrt{MS_E}\)exact \(\chi^2\), df \((n-1)(k-1)\)
SEMtwowayagreement\(\sqrt{(MS_J + (n-1) MS_E)/n}\)Satterthwaite \(\chi^2\)
SEMonewayagreement\(\sqrt{MS_W}\)exact \(\chi^2\), df \(n(k-1)\)
SEEanyany\(SD \sqrt{ICC(1 - ICC)}\)delta method, log scale
SEPanyany\(SD \sqrt{1 - ICC^2}\)delta method, log scale

The consistency SEM is the typical error of Hopkins (2000) and the \(\sqrt{MS_E}\) preferred by Weir (2005); the one-way SEM is the within-subject SD of Bland and Altman. The agreement SEM adds the variance between items to the error; with complete data it equals the one-way SEM, but its degrees of freedom differ.

SEE and SEP (Weir, 2005, eqs. 11 and 15) use the single-measure ICC of the same model and type (ICC(C,1), ICC(A,1) or ICC(1)). The SEE is the standard error of a subject's estimated true score; the SEP is used to judge whether a change from the estimated true score is real. Both depend on how much subjects differ from each other, so the SEM is generally the better description of measurement error.

Total SD. SD is the total SD matched to the denominator of the ICC: \(SD^2 = \sigma^2_{subjects} + \sigma^2_{error}\) for consistency, plus \(\sigma^2_{items}\) for agreement. With this SD, \(SD\sqrt{1 - ICC}\) equals the SEM exactly, which is why there is no separate ICC-based SEM. In mean squares (complete data): \(SD^2 = (MS_B + (k-1)MS_E)/k\) (consistency), \((MS_B + (k-1)MS_E + k(MS_J - MS_E)/n)/k\) (agreement), and \((MS_B + (k-1)MS_W)/k\) (one-way). It is not the SD of all the measurements, \(\sqrt{SS_{total}/(N-1)}\), used by Weir (2005) and by reli_stats(), which estimates none of these variances; so SEE and SEP differ slightly from Weir's (for his data set A, SD 32.83 vs 31.74, SEE 7.35 vs 7.11, SEP 10.54 vs 10.20). A negative ICC estimate is treated as zero (SEE = 0, SEP = SD).

Intervals and tests. The SEM interval is the square root of the \(\chi^2\) interval for the error variance, and the test of \(H_0: SEM = \) null.value is the \(\chi^2\) test of the variance, \(\nu \cdot SEM^2 / null^2\). For the SEE and SEP the interval is a Wald interval on the log scale, with a delta-method SE from the normal-theory variances of the mean squares, and the test is the matching z test. With a one-sided alternative the interval is one-sided. method = "reml" with missing data uses degrees of freedom based on the observed data, as in icc_test(), and gives a warning.

Bootstrap. boot = TRUE resamples subjects, as in icc_test(), including the hybrid step for the two-way agreement statistics (the item mean square of each replicate is multiplied by an independent \(\chi^2_{k-1}/(k-1)\) draw). The studentized interval works on the log scale. The p-value inverts the interval and is approximate.

In simulations (3 trials, 10 or 30 subjects, ICC 0.5 or 0.9, normal or skewed and heavy-tailed data, complete data), the analytic intervals covered 0.93 to 0.97 with normal data for the consistency and one-way statistics, but only 0.79 to 0.90 with non-normal data (the \(\chi^2\) interval for a variance is sensitive to heavy tails). The studentized bootstrap was the best method for the consistency SEM, the SEP and the one-way SEM (0.89 to 0.96 throughout), and BCa for the agreement SEM and SEP (mean 0.91), hence boot_ci = "auto". The percentile interval was too narrow with 10 subjects (as low as 0.54). For the SEE the analytic interval was best with normal data (0.93 to 0.97); no bootstrap interval was reliable near an ICC of 0.5, where the SEE hardly changes with the ICC.

Agreement statistics with few items. The agreement SEM and SEP include the variance between items, which is estimated from only k - 1 degrees of freedom. When it is a large part of the error and k is small, every interval under-covers: with 3 trials and an item variance about as large as the error variance (ICC 0.9), the Satterthwaite interval covered 0.81 to 0.91 with normal data and BCa 0.91 to 0.95 (0.80 with 30 subjects and skewed data). Resampling subjects without the hybrid step covered only 0.39 to 0.63 in those settings. More items help more than more subjects.

Coefficient of variation. When the error grows with the size of the measurements, it is better expressed relative to them (Hopkins, 2000; Atkinson and Nevill, 1998; Weir, 2005). Two scales are available:

  • scale = "log" fits the model to the natural logarithm of the measurements (all must be positive) and reports \(100 \times\) the statistic, in sympercents (Cole, 2000). Because this is a constant multiple of the log-scale statistic, the SEM keeps its exact (or Satterthwaite) \(\chi^2\) interval and test. A sympercent \(s\) converts to the conventional CV% as \(100\sqrt{\exp((s/100)^2) - 1}\); the two are nearly identical below about 15% (e.g. 10 sympercents is a CV of 10.03%). The conversion is monotone, so it can be applied to the interval limits too.

  • scale = "mean" reports \(100 \times\) statistic / grand mean (the "pooled" CV). The interval and test use the delta method on the log scale, adding the uncertainty in the grand mean, whose normal-theory variance is \(MS_B/(nk)\) with items fixed (consistency, one-way) and \((MS_B + MS_J - MS_E)/(nk)\) with items random (two-way agreement).

In simulations like those below (population mean 5), the "mean" interval covered 0.93 to 0.96 with normal data and 30 subjects (except for the agreement SEM with few items, see below); leaving out the uncertainty in the grand mean lowered coverage by up to 0.05. With the bootstrap, the grand mean of each replicate of a two-way agreement statistic also gets the item mean's normal-theory variation, as in the hybrid step below.

null.value is on the same scale as the estimate. The log scale is usually preferable: it treats the error as proportional to each measurement rather than to the overall mean.

Minimal detectable change. The minimal detectable change (MDC), smallest real difference, or repeatability coefficient is a scaled SEM: \(1.96 \sqrt{2} SEM\) for 95% (Weir, 2005, eq. 13). mdc_test() computes it, with its interval and a test, from the data or from an SEM result of this function. With two trials, agreement_limit() gives the same quantity as the half width of the limits of agreement, with the bias reported separately.

References

Atkinson, G., & Nevill, A. M. (1998). Statistical methods for assessing measurement error (reliability) in variables relevant to sports medicine. Sports Medicine, 26(4), 217-238. doi:10.2165/00007256-199826040-00002

Cole, T. J. (2000). Sympercents: symmetric percentage differences on the 100 log_e scale simplify the presentation of log transformed data. Statistics in Medicine, 19(22), 3109-3125. doi:10.1002/1097-0258(20001130)19:22<3109::AID-SIM558>3.0.CO;2-F

Hopkins, W. G. (2000). Measures of reliability in sports medicine and science. Sports Medicine, 30(1), 1-15. doi:10.2165/00007256-200030010-00001

Weir, J. P. (2005). Quantifying test-retest reliability using the intraclass correlation coefficient and the SEM. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 19(1), 231-240. doi:10.1519/15184.1

See also

icc_test(); reli_htest-methods for summary(), plot() and check().

Examples

# Weir (2005) data set A: 8 subjects, 2 trials
weir <- data.frame(t1 = c(146, 148, 170, 90, 157, 156, 176, 205),
                   t2 = c(140, 152, 152, 99, 145, 153, 167, 218))
reli_err_test(col.names = c("t1", "t2"), data = weir)
#> 
#> 	Standard error of measurement (two-way, consistency)
#> 
#> data:  t1, t2
#> 
#> alternative hypothesis: two.sided
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>   4.996445 15.380402
#> sample estimates:
#>      SEM 
#> 7.556927 
#> 

# Is the typical error below 10 units?
reli_err_test(col.names = c("t1", "t2"), data = weir, null.value = 10)
#> 
#> 	Standard error of measurement (two-way, consistency)
#> 
#> data:  t1, t2
#> X-squared = 3.9975, df = 7, p-value = 0.2199
#> alternative hypothesis: true SEM is less than 10
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>   0.00000 13.58094
#> sample estimates:
#>      SEM 
#> 7.556927 
#> 

# Typical error as a coefficient of variation (sympercents)
reli_err_test(col.names = c("t1", "t2"), data = weir, scale = "log")
#> 
#> 	Standard error of measurement (two-way, consistency), log scale
#> 	(sympercents)
#> 
#> data:  t1, t2
#> 
#> alternative hypothesis: two.sided
#> 95 percent confidence interval:
#>   3.327576 10.243176
#> sample estimates:
#> SEM (sympercent) 
#>         5.032829 
#> 

# Standard error of prediction
res <- reli_err_test(col.names = c("t1", "t2"), data = weir, stat = "SEP")
summary(res)
#> The estimated SEP was 10.5 (95% compatibility interval [6.33, 17.6]).
#> Values in this interval are the most compatible with the data, given
#> the model and its assumptions. The estimate is the standard error of
#> prediction (two-way, consistency), in the units of the measurement: the
#> standard error for judging change from a subject's estimated true
#> score, SD * sqrt(1 - ICC^2) with ICC(C,1) and the SD matched to its
#> denominator, excluding systematic differences between items. The data
#> had 8 subjects and 2 items (16 measurements, none missing); variance
#> components were estimated by analysis of variance. The interval uses
#> the delta method on the log scale with normal-theory variances of the
#> mean squares.
